item.title: Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade unveils medals, torch
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
Staff members display uniforms and equipment at the 100-day countdown event for the Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade in Changchun, northeast China's Jilin Province, Oct. 7, 2026. The medals, torch, uniforms and equipment for the Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade were unveiled on Wednesday at a 100-day countdown event held at the Changchun International Aviation Expo City. (Xinhua/Xu Chang) CHANGCHUN, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Medals, the torch, uniforms and equipment for the Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade were unveiled Wednesday at a 100-day countdown event at Changchun International Aviation Expo City. The torch, named "Ji Xiang," or "Auspicious Flight," is inspired by the clivia, Changchun's city flower. Its upper section features a filmstrip motif and 12 winter sports icons representing the Games' disciplines, a reference to Changchun's film industry. Snowflake and ginseng flower motifs appear near the top, while ski-inspired lines run down the sides and a wheel-hub pattern decorates the base. The torch stands 711 millimeters tall, a reference to the highest elevation in Changchun's urban area, 711 meters. The medals, named "Ji Meng," or "Auspicious Dream," combine traditional Chinese cultural elements, winter sports imagery and features associated with Changchun. The front features patterns inspired by skate blades and ski tracks, while the reverse depicts the "First Jade Bird of Ancient China," an artifact unearthed at the Wutaishan historic site in Nong'an, Changchun. Part of the bird design is inlaid with Songhua stone from Jilin. A filmstrip pattern along the medal's edge also references Changchun's film heritage. An embedded NFC chip allows athletes to access images of their medal ceremonies and seasonal scenery from Changchun by tapping the medal with a smartphone. Uniforms for torchbearers, torch escorts, volunteers, staff, technical delegates and ceremony personnel were also unveiled. The Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade will be held from January 15 to 25, with competitions in Changchun and nearby Jilin City. ■ The torch is unveiled at the 100-day countdown event for the Changchun 2027 Winter Universiade in Changchun, northeast China's Jilin Province, Oct. 7, 2026. item.title: Russian tourism industry eyes attracting more Chinese visitors
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
MOSCOW, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- During China's week-long National Day holiday this year, Chinese tourists are frequently seen on the streets of Moscow. "Russia is a unique country and a must-visit," said Wang Xinzuo, who visited several Russian cities and described his trip as smooth and enjoyable. In the first half of 2026, Chinese tourists accounted for over 50 percent of all inbound tourist trips to Russia. "We are witnessing a substantial rise in travel volumes. In 2025, the number of mutual tourist visits exceeded 3 million. According to our data, 154,200 Chinese tourists visited Russia in the first quarter alone this year, marking a 44 percent increase year on year," Chinese Ambassador to Russia Zhang Hanhui said before the holiday. Russia is preparing for further growth. In early September, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Chernyshenko said the country aims to accommodate more than 5.5 million Chinese tourists by 2030. Behind the figures lies an industry adapting to a new generation of Chinese travelers. MOSCOW: FROM GROUP TO INDEPENDENT TRAVEL Moscow remains the main gateway for Chinese tourists. According to the Border Service of the Russian Federation, 240,000 Chinese tourists visited Moscow in the first half of 2026, up 7 percent year on year. But the profile of visitors is changing. Guided group tours are becoming less dominant as younger and more independent Chinese travelers arrive. More than 80 percent of travelers from China come to Moscow independently, including for business, according to Bulat Nurmukhanov, deputy chairman of the Moscow Tourism Committee. In response, a China Friendly certification program is expanding in Moscow, covering services such as Chinese-language information, adapted menus and trained staff. The Cosmos Hotel Group told Xinhua that two of its four- and five-star hotels in Moscow have received the certification, with more properties planned to join the program. Moscow has also strengthened its promotion in China through Chinese-language tourism services, social media and cooperation with Chinese travel platforms, while highlighting its cultural heritage and modern attractions. REGIONS SEEK NEW OPPORTUNITIES Beyond Moscow, Russian regions are increasingly competing for Chinese tourists. In St. Petersburg, the number of Chinese tourists has risen by nearly 60 percent since 2021, according to Nana Gvichiya, deputy chair of the city's Tourism Development Committee. Chinese visitors are showing a growing interest not only in historical sites but also in local cuisine and creative spaces. In the Altai region, the number of Chinese tourists increased 1.5 times in 2025 from the previous year, exceeding 6,000 for the first time, said Alexander Baryshnikov, head of the regional Department for Tourism and Resort Development. Although the region receives fewer Chinese visitors than Moscow and St. Petersburg partly because of a lack of direct flights, local businesses are improving services and developing China-friendly tourism products. Several hotels and resorts have received China Friendly certification, while tour operators have developed specialized routes and promoted them through international exhibitions and Chinese social media. In Russia's Far East, the Amur region has recorded a 60 percent increase in Chinese tourists since the introduction of the visa-free policy between China and Russia in 2025, Governor Vasily Orlov said. The region plans more than 200 joint events with China in 2026. A planned cross-border cable car linking Blagoveshchensk and Heihe is also expected to boost tourism. Once completed, the journey between the two countries will take just over two minutes, with an annual capacity of 2.5 million passengers. ADAPTING SERVICES The rapid growth has also exposed gaps in Russia's tourism infrastructure. Experts and tourists cite language barriers, difficulties with digital payments and a shortage of qualified staff, particularly outside major tourist destinations. "Special attention should be paid to the training of professional guides for Chinese groups in Russia," said Anastasia Pavlova, an expert on cultural and tourism cooperation at the Russian State University for the Humanities. Ilya Umansky, president of the Russian Union of Tourism Industry, stressed the need for closer cooperation between the two sides in the tourism sector. "Today we find ourselves in a unique state of revival of our mutual tourist exchanges," Umansky said. "I am confident that we have a great future."■

item.title: Henri Kagan, Kenso Soai win 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry is announced in Stockholm, Sweden, Oct. 7, 2026. Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced Wednesday. (Xinhua/Lyu You) STOCKHOLM, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced on Wednesday. According to the Academy, some molecules, such as amino acids, exist in two variants that are mirror images of each other. However, living organisms only contain one of these mirror-image forms. How such chemical asymmetry, known as homochirality, could emerge had long remained a mystery to chemists. "This year's prize recognises discoveries that have enabled chemists to drive chemical reactions that lead to homochirality," the Academy said in a statement, noting that the two laureates "made chemistry choose a mirror image." "Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously. The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular," says Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry. Kagan, born in France on Dec. 15, 1930, is affiliated with Universite Paris-Sud in Orsay, France. Soai, born in Japan in 1950, is a professor at Tokyo University of Science. ■

item.title: Another Nanjing Massacre survivor dies, only 20 remain
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
NANJING, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- One more survivor of the Nanjing Massacre passed away on Wednesday, reducing the number of registered living survivors to 20, the Memorial Hall of the Victims in Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders said. Massacre survivor Guo Xiulan died at the age of 94, according to the memorial hall in Nanjing, the capital of east China's Jiangsu Province. Guo was born in 1932. According to survivor recollections documented by the museum, when the Nanjing Massacre took place after Japanese troops captured Nanjing on Dec. 13, 1937, Guo's parents took their three children to hide in an underground shelter along with neighbors. "Japanese soldiers stood at the opening and strafed it with machine guns. My parents and my youngest sister perished. Only my second sister and I survived," Guo was recorded as saying. The Nanjing Massacre unfolded over six weeks. Japanese soldiers killed approximately 300,000 Chinese civilians and unarmed soldiers in one of the most barbaric atrocities of World War II. Over the years, the number of survivors able to share firsthand accounts of the massacre has continued to decline. In 2014, China's top legislature designated Dec. 13 as the national memorial day for the victims of the Nanjing Massacre. The Chinese government has also preserved survivors' testimonies through written records and video recordings. Documents related to the massacre were inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2015. To date, only 20 living survivors of the Nanjing Massacre remain on the registry maintained by the Nanjing Association for Assistance to Victims of Japanese Aggression and Inheritance of Nanjing Massacre Historical Memory. ■

item.title: China Focus: Culture-infused tourism gains traction during National Day holiday
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
BEIJING, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- On the morning of Oct. 1, the first day of China's National Day holiday, the Confucius cruise ship slowly pulled away from a port in Jining, east China's Shandong Province, setting off for Nanyang ancient town on the city's southern outskirts. Named after the famous ancient Chinese philosopher Confucius, the ship was bound for a 2-hour-plus journey, passing stretches of the Grand Canal, the world's oldest artificial waterway system, which connects rivers in northern and eastern China and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2014. "We chose the cruise after seeing online that it offered a rich cultural experience," said Zhao Xiaojie from the provincial capital Jinan, as she and her 11-year-old son read the ancient texts on the cabin's decorations inspired by the Six Arts -- the six foundational disciplines of ancient Confucian education. Her choice reflects a broader trend during this year's National Day holiday, as cultural content is weighing more and more heavily in China's tourism products. NATIONAL DAY EXTRAVAGANZA "Cruises have operated on the same route before, but the Confucius incorporates many cultural elements and intangible cultural heritage experiences, turning it into a moving showcase of Confucianism on the Grand Canal," said Zhang Feng, head of the cruise route. The round-trip ticket includes shuttle services to scenic spots and admission to the Kangqian Bieyuan and Huji Qianzhuang attractions. Visitors can also watch a traditional fishermen's wedding ceremony and cormorant fishing performances in Nanyang ancient town, Zhang said. Such packages bring together Confucianism and the culture of the Grand Canal, he added. The unusual holiday calendar this year, with the Mid-Autumn Festival falling just three working days before the National Day holiday, has given fresh momentum to the integration of culture and tourism. Data from Chinese online travel platform Ctrip showed that one in 10 travelers chose to combine the two holidays by taking three days off to create a 13-day break. Nearly half of those taking an extended break traveled for more than eight days. The longer holidays have expanded the travel radius of Chinese tourists, bringing cultural and tourism products in more remote and lesser-known destinations into the spotlight. In Cangyuan Wa Autonomous County, southwest China's Yunnan Province, for example, tourists gathered at a square to pound freshly harvested rice and prepare new rice, filling the air with its aroma. "New rice festival activities and service facilities have been upgraded this year, allowing visitors to experience the authentic culture of the Wa ethnic group," said Li Lei, deputy general manager of the Cangyuan County Tourism Investment Company. Traditional culture is not the only draw. A growing number of travelers are also visiting landmarks associated with China's revolutionary history, driven in part by the patriotic sentiment associated with the National Day holiday. This year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, which lasted from 1934 to 1936. The arduous journey helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution. In Yudu County, east China's Jiangxi Province, the Memorial Park of the Starting Point of the Central Red Army's Long March has attracted large numbers of study-tour groups and is expected to receive nearly 300,000 visits during the seven-day holiday. Dai Bin, president of the China Tourism Academy, said the flow of visitors to revolutionary landmarks reflects people's emotional identification with the revolutionary traditions. When they travel, they don't just want to see history; they also want to draw deeper inspiration from the revolutionary legacy for their lives today, according to him. INNOVATION REMAINS KEY The trend has also fallen in line with a series of development plans China released recently. The 15th Five-Year Plan for culture and tourism development, released by the Ministry of Culture and Tourism in September, calls for deeper integration between culture and tourism and their mutually reinforcing development with other areas of the economy and society. It stresses supporting the development of distinctive cultural industries and tourism in former revolutionary base areas. Moreover, it calls for expanding the space for cultural and tourism development, with deeper integration moving from resource consolidation and product integration toward new business models and broader applications. Hong'an Township in Xiushan Tujia and Miao Autonomous County, southwest China's Chongqing Municipality, has put such innovation into practice, drawing 190,000 tourist visits in the first two days of the holiday. Leveraging the cultural appeal of Border Town, a novel by renowned Chinese writer Shen Congwen, as well as its unique location where three provincial-level regions meet, the township has developed immersive, scenario-based tourism offerings that combine folk experiences, local cuisine and the nighttime economy. In Shandong, seven cities have joined forces to combine seven popular online-literature IPs with the region's landscapes and historical sites, encouraging fans to turn fictional worlds into real-life travel destinations. The model uses storytelling familiar to Generation Z to breathe new life into traditional cultural and tourism resources, converting online popularity into real-world tourism consumption. "The route runs from west to east, so fans can take a high-speed train and visit a different 'chapter' every day, which is very convenient," said Liu Wei, a fan of online literature born in the 2000s. For industry insiders, such efforts to generate more immersive cultural tourist activities are also necessary. Wu Liyun, a professor at Beijing International Studies University, said scenic spots once relied mainly on ticket sales, which is often unsustainable today. "The core of the industry transformation lies in adding more experiential offerings and opportunities for secondary consumption, with the focus on everyday settings, local culture and lifestyle-oriented services," she said. GLOBAL DRAW The shift has appealed to inbound travelers as well. With China offering unilateral visa-free entry to citizens of 50 countries and full mutual visa exemptions with 29 countries, its tourism industry has also been working to offer overseas tourists a wider range of immersive trips centered on cultural experiences. In Jingdezhen, east China's Jiangxi Province, where the Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in July, growing numbers of overseas visitors are exploring historic sites, taking part in art workshops and browsing handicraft markets, while enjoying distinctive cafes and homestays. The city, known as the "Porcelain Capital," now offers a range of experiences for visitors seeking to explore its centuries-old ceramic traditions, according to Zhang Chen, a local tourism industry insider. Options include a one-day program combining an introduction to local ceramic culture with hands-on pottery making, or a three-day workshop led by inheritors of intangible cultural heritage. "Many overseas visitors now seek a deeper cultural connection, rather than simply sightseeing," Zhang said. In Beijing, veteran tourist guide Dou Junjie feels a similar trend. He provides guided bicycle tours along the Beijing Central Axis, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2024 that covers former imperial palaces and sacrificial structures. "More overseas visitors to Beijing would like to experience local life and learn about local culture," Dou said. According to Gao Zhengyang, a guest researcher with Jiangsu Su Merchants Bank, immersive travel across destinations is replacing sightseeing and photo stops, a wider range of trendy Chinese products is making its way onto tourists' shopping lists, and the mix of visitors is becoming more diverse. Gao said all of these trends point to improvements in the quality of "China Travel." Data from Ctrip shows that bookings for one-day tours by inbound tourists during this year's National Day holiday and the Mid-Autumn Festival holiday surged by over 400 percent year on year, with scenic spot ticket sales up more than 220 percent and train tickets more than 170 percent. Li Xinjian, a professor at the Beijing International Studies University, said the growth in inbound tourism during what is traditionally a peak season for domestic travel reflects the increasingly diverse experiences on offer. "Overseas tourists are finding that China offers not only beautiful scenery but also engaging cultural experiences," he said. For Wu Liyun, value-added services such as the cultural experiences in Jingdezhen and Beijing are particularly important, as they are far more appealing than standardized products and usually leave a much deeper impression on travelers. Wu believes Jingdezhen's model can be replicated in terms of how cultural content is presented. She cited her hometown of Linyi in Shandong Province, where willow weaving products are widely exported, and tourists can try their hand at the traditional craft and take their own creations home. "Every city has its own ways of life passed down through generations," she said. "What you are accustomed to in the place where you live can be incredibly fresh and novel to outsiders." ■

item.title: China's railways see holiday return peak amid vibrant tourism market
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07
Passengers are seen at the waiting hall of Tianjin Railway Station in north China's Tianjin, Oct. 7, 2026. As the National Day holiday is drawing to a close, return travel flows increase across the country. (Photo by Du Penghui/Xinhua) BEIJING, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- China's railways saw the peak of the holiday return rush on Wednesday, with 24.15 million passenger trips expected on the final day of the National Day holiday, amid strong travel demand and vibrant tourism activity across the country. A total of 2,449 additional passenger trains were scheduled on Wednesday to cope with the surge in demand, according to China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. On Tuesday, the country's railways handled 21.6 million passenger trips, marking the third consecutive day with more than 20 million journeys. Beijing, Guangzhou, Chengdu, Xi'an, Wuhan, Hangzhou, Chongqing and Shanghai were among the busiest cities for departures and arrivals, while passenger flows were particularly heavy on routes including Beijing-Shanghai, Wuhan-Shanghai, Wuhan-Shenzhen and Xi'an-Chengdu. Railway authorities across the country added services and expanded overnight operations to facilitate the return rush as China's tourism market remained vibrant during the seven-day holiday, with county-level destinations and nighttime consumption emerging as notable trends. County-level destinations gained popularity as travelers increasingly sought slower-paced and more immersive experiences away from major cities. From the coastal county of Lingshui in south China's Hainan Province to Mohe, a county-level city on the country's northern frontier, smaller destinations are drawing visitors with distinctive local experiences. Meanwhile, nighttime consumption flourished in many cities, with cultural performances, night markets, light shows and food fairs extending visitor stays and enriching holiday experiences. ■ Passengers are seen at the waiting hall of Shanghai Hongqiao Railway Station in east China's Shanghai, Oct. 7, 2026. item.title: Police officers stand guard at China's highest-altitude border police station
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-06
Head of the Pumaqangtang border police station arranges police equipment in Pumaqangtang Township in Shannan, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, Aug. 19, 2026. Pumaqangtang, China's highest township, has an average altitude of 5,373 meters, with oxygen levels less than a half of that at sea level. Here stands the Pumaqangtang border police station, the highest-altitude border police station in China. Police and auxiliary police officers here, with an average age of just over 30, hold their posts on the frigid, oxygen-thin plateau. item.title: Brewing new trails, Yunnan coffee carries Chinese aroma across Asia-Pacific
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-06
* Yunnan sits on the northern fringe of the global coffee-growing "bean belt," the equatorial zone between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn. For centuries, its rolling highlands were known as China's tea heartland. Over the past two decades, steady investment, improved farming techniques and booming domestic consumption have nurtured a thriving home-grown coffee industry. * Cross-border innovation in coffee culture is also taking shape across the Lancang-Mekong basin, which China shares with Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam. * While Southeast Asia remains at the heart of Yunnan's Asia-Pacific coffee trade, the beans are travelling much farther -- all the way to New Zealand, where they remain a niche but notable newcomer to the specialty-coffee scene. KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 6 (Xinhua) -- When Thomas Ooi first tasted Yunnan coffee in Beijing in 2015, its savory, almost beef-jerky-like character struck him as unusual. Back then, few in Malaysia's coffee scene had their eye on beans from Yunnan, a Chinese province better known for tea. A decade later, everything has changed. Ooi, founder of Ghostbird Coffee Roastery in Kuala Lumpur, imported his first batch of Yunnan specialty beans in 2025, put them on his cafe menu, and watched them sell out in just two months. The growing popularity reflects a broader regional shift, as coffee from China's mountainous southwest gains ground beyond its home market, finding new drinkers across the Asia-Pacific and opening fresh avenues for trade, cultural exchange and appreciation of taste. EMERGING COFFEE ORIGIN Yunnan sits on the northern fringe of the global coffee-growing "bean belt," the equatorial zone between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn. For centuries, its rolling highlands were known as China's tea heartland. Over the past two decades, steady investment, improved farming techniques and booming domestic consumption have nurtured a thriving home-grown coffee industry. Yunnan's coffee industry spans six core growing zones: Pu'er, Baoshan, Lincang, Dehong, Xishuangbanna and Nujiang, each boasting unique strengths in nurturing specialty coffee. In the first eight months of 2026, the province exported 11,000 tonnes of coffee with a total value of 450 million yuan (67 million U.S. dollars). "I think Yunnan is very interesting, not just because of the coffee varietals themselves. I think the producers from Yunnan are very innovative," Ooi said, sharing his plan to visit Yunnan's coffee farms at the end of this year's harvest season, which will bring along fellow roaster friends eager to see the plantations firsthand. Malaysia is among Yunnan's key Asian export destinations. According to the provincial international trade association, Yunnan coffee was exported to 43 countries and regions in 2025, with European and Asian countries being leading destinations for Yunnan's coffee shipments. Within Asia, Vietnam and Malaysia stand as the two major markets. CROSS-BORDER BLENDS For Hanoi coffee specialist Pham Duy Anh, Yunnan beans are steadily winning over Vietnamese consumers, with an increasing number of specialty cafes and roasters now offering them. He said their appeal lies in improving quality with each harvest and a range of processing methods that suit Vietnamese drinkers seeking new flavors. "Diverse processing methods like washed, natural, honey and anaerobic have kept the beans from being boxed into a single flavor profile, giving drinkers notes such as mild wine, raisin, guava, tea and watermelon," Anh said, depicting it as an advantage in a market that values diversity and personalization in the coffee experience. Trade ties between Yunnan and Vietnam have grown beyond simple commodity exchanges, creating an environment that has helped fuel the growing coffee trade between the two sides. Joint initiatives, including the China-Vietnam coffee festival, industry-led trade alliances, enterprise matchmaking and supply-chain field visits, have built deep industry-to-industry connections. At the Fourth China International Supply Chain Expo in Beijing in June, a 40-square-meter Yunnan-Vietnam-themed coffee booth drew wide attention by highlighting its edge in frontier-based cross-border coffee supply chains. Cross-border innovation in coffee culture is also taking shape across the Lancang-Mekong basin, which China shares with Myanmar, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia and Vietnam. Omar Ali, co-founder and general manager of SinoTaste, created "Mekong Coffee with Six Flavors," a multi-country blended coffee drawing beans from all six Lancang-Mekong nations, after sampling roughly 50 bean lots and testing dozens of formulas. "When you make a multi-origin blend, the point is not to make one origin stand out. It is about how these coffees complement each other and create something none could achieve on its own," Omar Ali said. "It mirrors partnerships: every country and culture carries distinct strengths; brought together, they produce new possibilities." TO GO FURTHER AFIELD While Southeast Asia remains at the heart of Yunnan's Asia-Pacific coffee trade, the beans are travelling much farther -- all the way to New Zealand, where they remain a niche but notable newcomer to the specialty-coffee scene. New Zealand's cafe culture has relied heavily on beans from established Latin American producers such as Brazil and Colombia. But Yunnan green beans have begun appearing at a handful of local roasteries, Radio New Zealand reported. MQ Coffee, based in Auckland, New Zealand's largest city, is among the businesses giving Yunnan coffee a foothold in New Zealand. Its co-owner, Wang Yanqi, said the beans have improved markedly in quality in recent years, just as international interest in China as a source of coffee has begun to grow. The company features Yunnan beans in its training and tasting sessions, putting them side by side with coffees from other origins to give participants a firsthand taste of Yunnan's distinctive flavor profiles. Wang noted that some Yunnan coffees have good sweetness and body, allowing their distinctive coffee character to shine through even with milk added. The company has organized study tours for New Zealand coffee professionals and enthusiasts to visit growing regions inside Yunnan, where they could gain direct insight into local coffee farming and processing practices. To turn overseas interest into repeat purchases, Yunnan coffee must become more competitive on quality, price and reliability of supply, Wang said. The quality of Yunnan coffee has improved significantly over the past decade, Ooi said. "Now we are learning about its taste profiles, but we want to understand them more deeply." (Video reporters: Li Shutong, Wang Jiawei, Zul and Jonathan Tham Yao Ming; Video editors: Zhao Tianlin, Liu Xiaorui, Zhang Yuhong and Zhang Yichi)■

item.title: Longer trips, richer experiences: China's National Day holiday reveals shifting tourism trends
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05
* Chinese travelers have ventured farther during the National Day holiday, with family trips and experience-oriented travel on the rise. * Former revolutionary base areas have drawn renewed interest from holidaymakers, with visits offering travelers a chance to learn about the country's revolutionary history and reflect on the difficult years that helped shape modern China. * More international travelers are flocking to China to experience the country for themselves, riding a rising wave of global fascination with everything from the scenery and culture to its lifestyles and, more recently, Chinese brands and design. BEIJING, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Five days into China's week-long National Day holiday, millions are still immersed in the sights, sounds and flavors of the season -- traveling, dining, exploring and enjoying the break. Yet this year, the scenes are subtly different. Travelers have ventured farther as the Mid-Autumn Festival holiday fell just three days before the National Day holiday, while family trips and experience-oriented travel are on the rise, according to travel agencies. "It points to a fundamental shift in the logic of tourism consumption, as travelers focus more on the quality of time and the richness of their experiences," said Bu Xiting, a researcher with the Communication University of China. LONGER BREAKS, RICHER CHOICES Data from Chinese online travel platform Tuniu shows that tours of 10 days or more are particularly popular during this holiday period, accounting for 26 percent of bookings. Yuan You, an internet company employee, spent three days of her 13-day break in Jiuzhaigou, southwest China's Sichuan Province, before heading to the provincial capital Chengdu for woodworking classes. "The holiday is rich while maintaining a relaxed pace," she said. Authorities across the country have rolled out a wide range of activities, consumer vouchers and subsidies to spur holiday spending. Shanghai, for example, has launched about 200 major consumption events, backed by consumer vouchers worth roughly 100 million yuan (around 14.85 million U.S. dollars). The offerings range from watching films and dining to purchasing digital products and cars, encouraging consumers to explore a broader spectrum of spending experiences. Cultural institutions, too, are broadening the ways people can experience and consume culture. The Sichuan Museum extended its holiday hours and launched a themed night tour, while Beijing's Zhongshan Park brought museums, cultural institutions and innovative brands together to create a market street featuring culture-inspired products. As more new energy vehicles hit the roads during the holiday, authorities have taken measures to ensure adequate charging facilities and convenient services. During last year's eight-day Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holiday period, Chinese travelers made 888 million domestic trips and spent a combined 809 billion yuan, according to the Ministry of Culture and Tourism. This year, data shows that foot traffic and revenue at 78 major shopping streets and commercial districts monitored by the Ministry of Commerce rose 3.4 percent and 5.3 percent year on year, respectively, from Oct. 1 to 3. RED TOURISM, ROBOTS AND RURAL EXPERIENCES As China marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, former revolutionary base areas have drawn renewed interest from holidaymakers, with visits offering travelers a chance to learn about the country's revolutionary history and reflect on the difficult years that helped shape modern China. In Yan'an, northwest China's Shaanxi Province, a street has staged special activities including performances of songs from the revolutionary years and a large-scale bonfire gathering. Visitor numbers on the first day of the holiday rose about 20 percent year on year. The holiday has also turned some of China's newest robots into part of the consumer experience, putting embodied intelligence to work alongside traditional culture in tourist attractions, shopping districts and ancient towns. At a cultural district in Chengdu, robots performed dances inspired by local opera's face-changing art and used digital technology to recreate tanghua, a traditional form of sugar painting. On Chunxi Road, a humanoid robot has gone beyond entertainment to take on the role of a store manager, greeting customers and recommending products rather than simply performing for them. China's growing network of robot training bases is preparing more machines for roles beyond the factory floor -- and beyond the country's borders. In the first half of 2026, Chinese manufacturers accounted for 97 percent of humanoid robot shipments worldwide, according to a report released at the 2026 World Robot Conference. Years of efforts to restore the environment and revitalize rural areas are also paying off. On a ridge overlooking the Miyun Reservoir in Beijing, visitors can hike to a viewing platform and enjoy outdoor concerts amid the pine trees. With roads, infrastructure and public services extending deeper into the countryside, some once-remote villages are emerging as new destinations for holidaymakers. Caijiagou, a former impoverished hillside village in east China's Shandong Province, has transformed into an art-themed destination, with murals adorning residential walls. Village official Liang Yunhui said the village has repurposed idle rural homes into cultural spaces such as an art gallery and a musical instrument museum, while hosting events featuring traditional crafts, cultural fairs and folk music. "In total, we have received more than 500,000 visits over the years," he said. On travel platform Fliggy, the number of users purchasing travel products featuring natural scenery and villages surged by nearly 50 percent from the same holiday period last year. "More travelers are seeking immersive experiences, from sampling local cuisine and making intangible cultural heritage crafts to watching distinctive performances, allowing them to gain a deeper appreciation of local culture," said a manager with Tuniu. CHINA HAUL While many Chinese tourists are venturing farther around the world, more international travelers are flocking to China to experience the country for themselves, riding a rising wave of global fascination with everything from the scenery and culture to its lifestyles and, more recently, Chinese brands and design. Tennis star Novak Djokovic, in Beijing for the China Open, was seen trying his hand at Chinese calligraphy at the Summer Palace, a former imperial garden. After a match, he used a traditional Chinese seal to put his mark on fans' keepsakes instead of signing autographs. Huaqiangbei, a sprawling electronics marketplace in south China's tech hub Shenzhen, has become a magnet for foreign shoppers looking to experience China's tech scene firsthand. Bryan Lamothe-Arice from the United States was browsing smart devices. "I'm particularly interested in the electric bikes and all kinds of flying devices here. I'm going to tell my friends to come here. There are tech products everywhere." China's border crossings are expected to see about 2.15 million passenger trips a day on average during the National Day holiday, according to the National Immigration Administration. That growing international interest is also showing up in spending. Overseas visitors spent 263.6 billion yuan in China in the first seven months of 2026, up 27.8 percent year on year, according to the commerce ministry. (Video reporters: Chen Si, Lin Long, Ji Zijian, Sun Qing and Zhong Chao; Video editors: Zhang Mocheng and Hong Ling) ■
